content: 1. A study published in the International Journal of Hygiene and Environmental Health in 2017 (Volume 220, Issue 8, Pages 1333–1339) examined respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) surveillance over an 18-year period, highlighting its impact on children. 2. Bruden, Singleton, and Hawk conducted an 18-year surveillance study on respiratory syncytial virus, with findings published in the Pediatric Infectious Disease Journal in 2015 (Volume 34, Issue 9, Pages 945–950). 3. Ferrer et al. developed a hierarchical model to investigate risk factors for childhood diarrhea in a middle-income country. Their case-control study was published in the International Journal of Epidemiology in 2008 (Volume 37, Issue 4, Pages 805–815). 4. Quigley, Cumberland, Cowden, and Rodrigues explored the protective effects of breastfeeding against diarrheal disease in infants in 1990s England. Their case-control study appeared in the Archives of Disease in Childhood in 2006 (Volume 91, Issue 3, Pages 245–250). 5. Mourad examined the association between living conditions in Palestinian refugee camps and the prevalence of intestinal parasites and diarrhea. This case study, focusing on the Nuseirat refugee camp, was published in Public Health in 2004 (Volume 118, Issue 2, Pages 131–142). 6. Harper et al. assessed the burden of acute gastrointestinal illness in two Inuit communities in Canada, with results published in Epidemiology and Infection in 2015 (Volume 143, Issue 14, Pages 3048–3063). 7. Okour, Al-Ghazawi, and Gharaibeh investigated the prevalence of diarrhea among children and its association with household conditions in a low-income rural community in the Jordan Valley. Their findings were published in the Jordan Medical Journal in 2012 (Volume 46, Issue 2). 8. Ramani, Fruhauf, and Dutta studied the relationship between adolescent diarrhea and school toilet conditions in an Indian village. Their findings were published in the Journal of Development Studies in 2017 (Volume 53, Issue 11, Pages 1899–1914). 9. El-Gilany and Hammad analyzed the epidemiology of diarrheal diseases among children under five years in Dakahlia, Egypt. Their study appeared in the Eastern Mediterranean Health Journal in 2005 (Volume 11, Issue 4, Pages 762–775). 10. Monasta, Andersson, Ledogar, and Cockcroft conducted a case study on the health of children living in five foreign Romá camps in Italy, focusing on minority health and epidemiology. Their findings were published in the American Journal of Public Health in 2008 (Volume 98, Issue 11, Pages 2035–2041). 11. Pezzani et al. investigated intestinal parasitoses among suburban and rural schoolchildren in Argentina, with results published in Revista Patología Tropical in 2012 (Volume 41, Pages 63–73). 12. Mohan et al. reported on rotavirus infection and disease in a multisite birth cohort as part of the MAL-ED Study. Their findings were published in the Journal of Infectious Diseases in 2017 (Volume 216, Issue 3, Pages 305–316). 13. Etiler, Velipasaoglu, and Aktekin identified risk factors for overall and persistent diarrhea in infancy in Antalya, Turkey. Their cohort study was published in Public Health in 2004 (Volume 118, Issue 1, Pages 62–69). 14. Kyle et al. explored the relationship between childhood disadvantage and emergency admission rates for common conditions in London. Their exploratory analysis was published in the Archives of Disease in Childhood in 2011 (Volume 96, Issue 3, Pages 1093–1096). 15. Mirabel et al. conducted echocardiography screening to detect rheumatic heart disease among schoolchildren in the French Pacific Islands. Their cohort study was published in the International Journal of Cardiology in 2015 (Volume 188, Pages 89–95). 16. Jaine, Baker, and Venugopal examined the association between household crowding and acute rheumatic fever in a developed country. Their findings were published in the Pediatric Infectious Disease Journal in 2011 (Volume 30, Issue 4, Pages 315–319). 17. Okello et al. investigated socioeconomic and environmental risk factors among rheumatic heart disease patients in Uganda. Their study was published in PLOS ONE in 2012 (Volume 7, Issue 8, Pages 3–8). 18. Riaz et al. identified risk factors for rheumatic heart disease in Bangladesh through a case-control study. Their findings were published in the Journal of Health, Population, and Nutrition in 2013 (Volume 31, Issue 1, Pages 70–77). 19. Phillips and Osmond analyzed whether susceptibility to chronic rheumatic heart disease is determined in early infancy, using mortality data from 20th-century Britain. Their study appeared in Global Cardiology Science and Practice in 2014 (Issue 4, Pages 464–472). 20. Hosoglu et al. identified risk factors for typhoid fever among adult patients in Diyarbakir, Turkey. Their findings were published in Epidemiology and Infection in 2006 (Volume 134, Issue 3, Pages 612–616). 21. Alemayehu, Mekasha, and Abebe studied the nasal carriage rate and antibiotic susceptibility patterns of Neisseria meningitidis in healthy Ethiopian children and adolescents. Their cross-sectional study was published in PLOS ONE in 2017 (Volume 12, Issue 10, Article e0187207). 22. Olea et al. conducted a case-control study on risk factors for meningococcal disease in Chile. Their findings were published in Emerging Infectious Diseases in 2017 (Volume 23, Issue 7, Pages 1070–1078). 23. Norheim et al. analyzed the association between smoking prevalence and meningococcal disease incidence in Norway, Sweden, Denmark, and the Netherlands from 1975 to 2009. Their population-based time series analysis was published in BMJ Open in 2014 (Volume 4, Issue 2, Article e003312). 24. De Wals et al. evaluated the effectiveness of the serogroup C meningococcal polysaccharide vaccine in Quebec through a case-control study. Their findings were published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2005 (Volume 40, Issue 8, Pages 1116–1122). 25. Deutsch et al. identified crowding as a risk factor for meningococcal disease in Danish preschool children. Their nationwide population-based case-control study was published in the Scandinavian Journal of Infectious Diseases in 2004 (Volume 36, Issue 1, Pages 20–23).
